item.title: Lil Scrappy Shares Hospital Gifts Post With Khaotic After Prayer Appeal
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Lil Scrappy and Khaotic shared a hospital gifts post after his prayer request, following recent Atlanta appearances.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Scrappy and Khaotic shared a joint Instagram post about a hospital visit on November 6, two days after a report that Scrappy had asked fans to pray for him.

The caption read, “Scrappy Reaction To My Gifts In The Hospital.” Khaotic’s verified account was listed alongside Scrappy’s on the post.

Scrappy had shared a hospital video through Instagram Stories and requested prayers. The reason for his visit and a discharge date remain unverified.

Before those posts, Scrappy performed during Game 3 of the WNBA Finals at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena on October 21. His appearance came during a break in the game as the Atlanta Dream hosted the Golden State Valkyries.

He then appeared on an October 28 episode of “Everyone Watches Women’s Sports.” The show’s description identified him as a guest discussing the Game 3 atmosphere and the Finals schedule.

The episode was released a week before the hospital prayer request was reported.

His Instagram account also continued promoting music that week. In a post announcing a Friday video release for “Smackin,” Scrappy named Bambi, Bobby V and Pleasure P among the people appearing in it.

Scrappy’s previous hospitalizations include an asthma attack in April 2012. He was taken to Emory University Hospital after waking up struggling to breathe and speak. His account described needing help from the people around him, including his mother and driver.

He was treated and released, then said he had obtained a breathing machine that he planned to keep with him. No connection between that asthma episode and the current hospital visit has been established.

Another hospital stay followed a car crash in the Miami area on June 3, 2018.

Scrappy suffered a broken foot in the wreck, which also involved a friend. He later shared a recovery update on Instagram while family members supported him at the hospital.

He left the hospital June 11, 2018, after eight days, with rehabilitation ahead for a foot broken in seven places.

Scrappy is also among the returning cast members interviewed for “Love & Hip Hop: The Final Chapter.” The six-part retrospective premieres November 10 at 8 P.M. ET on VH1, BET and MTV, with weekly episodes across all three networks.

item.title: Soulja Boy Says Toy Shop Passes $1M In Sales, Debuts Big Drip Plushie With Hilarious YouTube Series
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Soulja Boy says his toy shop passed one million in sales as a $50 made-to-order plush remains open for preorder.
item.content:encoded:
Soulja Boy says his online toy shop has crossed a seven-figure sales mark, but the rapper’s brief announcement leaves the unit behind that number open.

In a post from his verified Snapchat account, Soulja Boy wrote, “Over 1 Million in sales,” and directed viewers to the Soulja Boy DripCo store.

The store’s current big push is a $50 plush Soulja Toy, named Big Drip. Its product page describes the item as made to order and sets a November 25 preorder deadline.

“The newest superstar in the toy world has arrived! 🎬✨ Big personality. Big style. BIG DRIP! From music to fashion to toys, we’re building an empire,” Soulja Boy wrote in an announcement.

The rap star also revealed a new cartoon series to go along with the toy, “Soulja Toy Adventures.”

Buyers also do not get a fixed delivery date on the page. The store says it will provide estimated delivery updates later, a meaningful detail for customers considering the toy during the holiday shopping season.

Other items up for sale include a Soulja Boy TikTok shirt, DropCo joggers, Soulja Boy camo sneakers and more.

Soulja Boy has spent years extending his name beyond records into merchandise and consumer products and now with Soulja Toy, he is aiming to take a bite out of the $14 billion plushie market.

item.title: GS Boyz’s “Stanky Legg” Becomes A Chicago Bears Victory Signal
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A 2008 GS Boyz dance record has become the Chicago Bears' locker-room victory signal as coach Ben Johnson keeps bringing it back.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears are carrying a 2008 Dallas rap dance into one of the NFL’s hottest locker rooms, where coach Ben Johnson’s version of the Stanky Legg now signals another win.

Chicago beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 27-24 on Sunday night, improving to 7-2 with its fourth straight victory. The team posted another edition of Johnson’s locker-room speech after the game, extending a season in which the coach’s celebrations have become part of the weekly story.

The dance started after Chicago’s 27-7 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on September 28. ESPN reported that Bears players were waiting for Johnson when he entered the locker room, leaving him to improvise.

“Honestly, I had no idea. Those guys were waiting for me like that, and so I didn’t know what to do,” Johnson said.

He rolled one leg, crossed an arm over his chest and gave the room a loose version of the dance that GS Boyz popularized with “Stanky Legg.”

The basic move shifts the dancer’s weight before the extended leg rolls in a loose circle. Johnson remembered high school teammates doing it in the 2000s, while his players immediately treated the awkward first attempt as something worth repeating.

The ritual survived beyond that Monday night win. Caleb Williams and other Bears joined Johnson after an October 22 victory over New England.

Johnson added a stutter-step after Chicago beat Seattle on November 2, and players began waiting for the dance as part of the team’s established “Good, Better, Best” postgame chant.

The Hip-Hop reference reaches back to Arlington, Texas, where GS Boyz turned “Stanky Legg” into a national dance record.

Billboard reported in 2009 that the single sold 443,000 downloads, reached No. 17 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs and peaked at No. 49 on the Hot 100. Nearly two decades later, the record’s signature move has found another audience inside an NFL locker room.

Johnson’s version is still more enthusiasm than precision, and Bears players have said it keeps improving. With Chicago entering the second half of its schedule at 7-2, every repeat now carries the same simple message: the team won again.

item.title: André 3000 Drops New Music – For Moncler
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: André 3000 scored Moncler's Re/Icons film and helped turn its mountain theme into a hands-on piece of visual art.
item.content:encoded:
André 3000 has turned a Moncler campaign into his latest music and visual-art experiment, scoring a new Re/Icons film while helping shape the images around it.

The Outkast co-founder supplied an unreleased piece for the film, making the campaign his first new music since 7 piano sketches arrived in May 2025.

Moncler has not named the track or announced a wider release, so for now the piece belongs to the film rather than a new single or album rollout.

The music is only one part of his contribution. During the shoot, André 3000 used white chalk to draw a mountain landscape across a black studio backdrop. That spontaneous image became the foundation for Moncler’s message: make a path instead of following one.

He also proposed carrying most of the Re/Icons collection at once, stacking jackets and expedition gear into a sculptural load that recalled the equipment early mountaineers carried.

Photographer and filmmaker Gabriel Moses captured the campaign, which presents André 3000 as a participant in the creative process instead of a celebrity placed in front of a finished concept.

Re/Icons revisits four pieces from Moncler’s archive: the Karakorum, Verone, Himalaya and Tibb. The 2026 edition expands the project beyond outerwear with windbreakers, shirts, pants, skirts and accessories. It is the first time the archive program has grown into a full ready-to-wear collection.

Moncler frames the range as a bridge between its expedition archive and a broader everyday wardrobe.

The line reached stores worldwide on October 15 after previews in Paris, Tokyo and New York. Cher, Grace Jones and JENNIE appeared in the campaign’s opening chapter before André 3000 joined the series with a separate film and set.

The project also extends the musician’s recent practice of moving between sound, design and performance.

The seven-song, 16-minute 7 piano sketches followed his 2023 instrumental album New Blue Sun, while his revived Benji Bixby fashion line returned during the 2025 Met Gala. The new score is brief, but it keeps that cross-disciplinary work moving.

His Moncler work folds those interests together in one short project, placing unheard André 3000 music inside a visual world he helped build with his own hands.

item.title: Black Dana White With Actual Qualifications Dismisses Congratulatory Messages As Trump Faces Wrong-Name Speculation
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Dana W. White corrected congratulatory messages as Trump's UFC job offer drew speculation about the former Pentagon spokeswoman.
item.content:encoded:
Dana W. White had already answered questions for Donald Trump‘s Pentagon. Now she was answering congratulations meant for the UFC boss who shares her name, as speculation spread that the president’s press secretary offer involved a mix-up.

The former Pentagon chief spokesperson addressed the confusion on LinkedIn after Trump offered UFC executive Dana White the White House job. Her response drew attention to a communications career that included speaking for Defense Secretary Jim Mattis during Trump’s first term.

“To everyone texting me congratulations: thank you, but you have the wrong Dana White,” she wrote.

White served as Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs from April 2017 through December 2018. She advised the secretary

and deputy secretary on communications, news media relations and public outreach while serving as the department’s chief spokesperson.

“I’ve stood at a podium and taken questions from the Pentagon press corps. I have never stood in an octagon. I’d like to keep it that way.”

Her Pentagon responsibilities extended well beyond the briefing room. She provided communications guidance for more than 4,500 public affairs personnel worldwide and directly oversaw the Defense Media Activity, an organization of roughly 2,000 employees serving military personnel and their families.

Those credentials gave the online theory a specific comparison: one Dana White had already held a senior government press position, while the Dana White Trump publicly named had built his career promoting combat sports. Social media users questioned whether a recommendation for the former spokeswoman had been misunderstood.

“It is nice for once that, that Dana White is being confused with this Dana White.”

Trump’s announcement explicitly referred to the UFC executive and proposed bringing fighters into his operation. The suggestion that the president confused the two remained online speculation, with no verified shortlist establishing that Dana W. White had been considered.

Her experience included Republican politics, national security and corporate communications. She began her Washington career as a House Republican Conference press secretary, later advised John McCain’s 2008 presidential campaign and worked on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

She also worked as a Wall Street Journal editorial writer in Hong Kong, a Fox News publicist and the Heritage Foundation’s director of the Washington Roundtable for the Asia-Pacific Press. She earned a University of Chicago degree in East Asian Languages and Civilization and speaks Mandarin Chinese and French.

Outside government, White held a communications leadership position with the Renault-Nissan Alliance in Paris and later became chief communications officer of Hyundai Motor North America. Her work there covered Hyundai and Genesis operations. She subsequently held a senior role at Ankura, and the National Bureau of Asian Research lists her as managing partner at Juno Collective.

Her Pentagon record also included an ethics investigation. A 2019 Defense Department inspector general report substantiated that she misused subordinates’ time for personal services and improperly accepted gifts. Her attorney disputed the findings, arguing that the tasks supported the office’s work. Investigators did not substantiate an allegation that she failed to treat subordinates with respect.

White closed her LinkedIn response with a wish for whoever ultimately takes the White House position: “Best of luck to the next White House Press Secretary!”

item.title: Grandmaster Melle Mel Lands 2027 Songwriters Hall Of Fame Nomination
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Grandmaster Melle Mel reaches the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame ballot as voters weigh a catalog that changed rap writing.
item.content:encoded:
Grandmaster Melle Mel has reached the ballot for the Songwriters Hall of Fame’s 2027 class, putting one of rap’s foundational writers before the organization’s voting members.

The official nomination list places Melvin Glover in the performing-songwriter category. It points voters to “The Message,” “Freedom,” “New York New York,” “Scorpio” and “White Lines (Don’t Do It)” as a sample of his catalog.

His place on this ballot focuses attention on the writing itself. Melle Mel helped move rap beyond party records by putting city pressure, poverty and survival into songs built for a mass audience. That work gave later MCs another model for what a record could carry.

A Library of Congress essay on “The Message” credits Melle Mel as a co-writer and vocalist. The 1982 record paired his verses with Duke Bootee’s writing and performance, turning a stark account of urban life into a national hit and a lasting part of Hip-Hop’s social vocabulary.

The Library of Congress placed the recording in the first National Recording Registry class in 2002, citing its focus on urban social issues and the path it opened for later rappers.

The nomination also adds another institution to his record. Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five became the first rap group inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2007. The Songwriters Hall now has to decide whether Melle Mel’s individual writing catalog belongs in its next class.

Hip-Hop and R&B have several lanes on the 2027 ballot. Kandi Burruss and will.i.am appear in the songwriter category, while Ne-Yo joins Melle Mel among performing songwriters.

Production duo Stargate is also nominated for a catalog that includes major records for Beyoncé, Rihanna and Ne-Yo.

A nomination starts the voting stage. The Hall says writers become eligible 20 years after the first commercial release of a notable song. Eligible members may choose up to three nominees in each category, and ballots are due by midnight Eastern on December 14.

Hip-Hop’s history inside the organization is still relatively short. Jay-Z became its first rapper inductee in 2017, decades after the culture began changing popular songwriting.

Melle Mel’s 2027 bid asks voters to recognize a writer whose words helped spark that change early on.

item.title: Jakiyra Metcalf Seeks Ole Miss Response To Racist Doorstep Harassment
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jakiyra Metcalf asked Ole Miss to respond after her doorbell camera recorded racist noises and gestures outside her home.
item.content:encoded:
The University of Mississippi responded after a doorbell camera recorded two women making monkey noises and gestures outside of Jakiyra Metcalf’s apartment, which she shares with two other Black women.

The recording carries an 8:37 P.M. timestamp from November 6. One woman jumps into view, beats her chest and makes the noises. A second moves closer to the camera and repeats them. A third walks behind the pair but does not appear to join in, according to the footage described by TheGrio.

Metcalf posted the clip on TikTok and tagged Ole Miss.

“What do we have to say about this ??” she wrote. She later added, “We just found out they are our upstairs neighbors,” and said she would share an update when she received one.

“We are committed to maintaining a safe and welcoming environment for all of our students, faculty, staff, and visitors and will follow our processes to ensure the well-being and safety of our community,” the university said, adding that an investigation is underway.

That location raises a direct safety concern beyond the viral reaction. The conduct happened at the students’ home, where avoiding the people in the recording may not be simple if Metcalf’s account of the neighbor relationship is accurate.

The university already publishes a process for incidents involving alleged racial bias. Its Campus Climate Concern Form defines bias-related incidents as alleged harassment, intimidation or threats motivated in whole or in part by race and other protected identities.

The page says a response team reviews submissions to connect affected people with support.

Ole Miss also makes clear that the response team is not a disciplinary body. The university says its student conduct office, campus police or equal-opportunity officials decide whether they have jurisdiction and whether a possible policy or legal violation should be investigated.

Those published steps establish a route for review but do not show that any office has opened a case involving Metcalf’s video.

The footage arrives two years after another racist gesture drew scrutiny at Ole Miss.

In May 2024, a white counterprotester was recorded making monkey noises and gestures toward a Black graduate student during a campus demonstration.

His fraternity removed him, and the university opened a student conduct investigation.

Metcalf’s video has now reached millions of viewers while she waits for a response. The university has not announced any disciplinary outcome or verified identification of the women in the official materials reviewed for this report.

item.title: Blueface Rubs His Sweaty Crotch With Towel & Throws It To Excited Woman
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Blueface threw a towel into a concert crowd after wiping it inside his shorts, as tour listings promoted other forms of fan access.
item.content:encoded:
Blueface wiped a towel inside his shorts and threw it into a concert crowd, where a woman near the front caught it,

The footage showed the shirtless rapper first using the white towel on his face and upper body. He then pushed it past his waistband and wiped his groin before sending it toward the audience, where several hands reached for it.

The clip circulated as Blueface promoted live appearances that leaned into his work as a streamer.

An official listing for his November 6 Colorado Springs booking used the name Streamers High Tour.

The Sunshine Studios Live ticket offer included a VIP package built around fan access, with a separate viewing area, priority entry, a post-show photo opportunity and a commemorative laminate.

The woman in the crowd, sitting front row, seemed to get more than her money’s worth and now has a unique keepsake to go along with her viral fame.

Blueface has also worked with fellow rapper and streamer DDG. AllHipHop previously reported that the two were billed together on the second leg of the Fresh Out of Love Tour, whose promotion drew on their online followings.

Blueface and DDG have a November 11 Miami appearance as well as upcoming stops in Amarillo, San Antonio, Austin, Chicago, Green Bay and Los Angeles.

item.title: Suno Says Artist Names Are Shorthand For genres In High-Stakes Legal Battle
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Suno sought dismissal of musicians' identity-rights claims, arguing artist-name prompts describe musical styles in its AI tool.
item.content:encoded:
Suno asked a federal judge to throw out musicians’ identity-rights claims, arguing that artist names entered into its AI music tool describe a sound.

The company filed its motion in Boston federal court in the proposed class action led by Jason Isbell.

“When people describe styles of music, they often use artists’ names as shorthand for the genre they perform in,” the filing states.

Suno says it converts those names into descriptions before sending instructions to its model.

The musicians accuse it of exploiting their identities without consent. Suno also raised First Amendment and federal copyright preemption defenses.

Isbell filed the lawsuit August 31 with David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle. It includes claims under state identity and biometric privacy laws.

Rap producers’ signatures have already become part of the wider legal fight over AI music. Music publisher Reservoir accused Suno of generating tracks with producer tags, the brief audio identifiers heard across Hip-Hop records.

Its copyright lawsuit covered 1,050 works and sought $157.5 million.

Reservoir alleged that Suno split recordings into vocal and backing tracks and used those parts, along with cover versions, to train its tools. The publisher also sought orders to stop the copying and destroy unlicensed copies.

The publisher challenged both the copying of recorded music during training and the appearance of producers’ audio signatures in newly generated tracks.

Suno has also been fighting over evidence in the copyright case brought by Universal Music Group and Sony Music. Apple Music asked a judge to limit testimony about its business after supplying information on AI songs available through the service.

Apple said Suno’s questions reached private licensing and royalty arrangements.

In its October 27 response, Suno tied four narrowed areas of questioning to its defenses. Those areas included label licensing and AI talks, Apple’s ability to operate without major catalogs, streaming fraud and communications about the case.

The company argued that the labels used their catalogs to seek restrictions on AI-generated music.

Judge Angel Kelley approved a schedule giving the musicians until December 1 to respond. Suno’s reply is due December 15.

item.title: Trey Songz Withdraws Promoter Lawsuit After Seeking Over $500K
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Trey Songz withdrew his lawsuit against Texas promoter Darryl Austin without prejudice, leaving the door open to refile.
item.content:encoded:
Trey Songz has withdrawn a lawsuit seeking more than $500,000 from a Texas promoter over a Fort Worth concert that never went ahead as planned.

The dismissal was filed “without prejudice,” according to MyNewsLA, leaving room for the dispute with Darryl Austin to return to court. The case was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court.

That type of dismissal allows a plaintiff to bring the same claims again, subject to filing deadlines. Those time limits keep running after a case is withdrawn.

Trey Songz Productions LLC brought the breach-of-contract case after a planned August 8 appearance at Will Rogers Auditorium fell apart.

AllHipHop covered the company’s demand in August, when the dispute centered on missed payments and the decision to move the show.

Under the deal finalized April 16, Austin was to pay a quarter of the performance fee the next day, another quarter on July 8 and the balance before the concert. The suit alleged the fee was fixed regardless of ticket sales.

The company said Austin paid the first installment but missed the second. He then sought a postponement, setting off a disagreement over both the money and whether the performance should go ahead.

Songz’s team said it had offered help with promotion and believed Austin had not done enough to sell the event. The singer’s side rejected the proposed delay and demanded the next payment under the agreement.

The lawsuit alleged that Austin still pushed the show to an undetermined date. Fans looking for tickets saw a postponement notice on Ticketmaster, while Songz’s side complained that the notice did not explain who made the decision.

The company sought damages for the unpaid performance fee, lost premium meet-and-greet income and harm to its reputation and future earning power. It also sought legal costs.

Austin challenged the California proceedings while representing himself. He described the concert fight as a “Texas-centered dispute” in a motion seeking to quash service of the summons.

Austin said he lived in Texas, had not visited California in about a decade and handled the negotiations by phone and email from Texas. His motion had been set for a November 19 hearing before Judge Phu Nguyen.
